claim: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified thousands of variants associated with human diseases and traits.
source: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified thousands of variants associated with human diseases and traits.
evidence: This is a general statement about GWAS findings that is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The majority of GWAS-implicated variants are in non-coding regions of the genome.
source: However, the majority of GWAS-implicated variants are in non-coding regions of the genome and require in depth follow-up to identify target genes and decipher biological mechanisms.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the GWAS literature and is supported by scientific knowledge.

claim: A pooled loss-of-function screen in primary hematopoietic cells was used to interrogate 389 candidate genes contained in 75 loci associated with red blood cell traits.
source: Here, rather than focusing on causal variants, we have undertaken a pooled loss-of-function screen in primary hematopoietic cells to interrogate 389 candidate genes contained in 75 loci associated with red blood cell traits.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: The screen identified 77 genes at 38 GWAS loci.
source: Using this approach, we identify 77 genes at 38 GWAS loci, with most loci harboring 1–2 candidate genes.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental screen reported in the manuscript.

claim: Most loci harbor 1-2 candidate genes.
source: Using this approach, we identify 77 genes at 38 GWAS loci, with most loci harboring 1–2 candidate genes.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the screen results.

claim: The hit set was strongly enriched for genes validated through orthogonal genetic approaches.
source: Importantly, the hit set was strongly enriched for genes validated through orthogonal genetic approaches.
evidence: This is a validation finding comparing the screen results to independent genetic data.

claim: Genes identified by this approach are enriched in specific and relevant biological pathways.
source: Genes identified by this approach are enriched in specific and relevant biological pathways, allowing regulators of human erythropoiesis and modifiers of blood diseases to be defined.
evidence: This is a finding from pathway analysis of the identified genes.

claim: Published GWAS successes have required in-depth mechanistic studies of individual loci and implicated genes to decipher biological mechanisms.
source: Despite these advances, our ability to discern the underlying biological mechanisms for the vast majority of such robust associations has remained limited, with a few exceptions (Claussnitzer et al., 2015; Gupta et al., 2017; Mohanan et al., 2018; Musunuru et al., 2010; Sankaran et al., 2008; Smemo et al., 2014). In general, published successes have required in-depth mechanistic studies of individual loci and implicated genes to decipher biological mechanisms.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Massively parallel reporter assays can be used to examine allelic variation.
source: Approaches that have shown the most success include the use of massively parallel reporter assays to examine allelic variation (Tewhey et al., 2016; Ulirsch et al., 2016; Vockley et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Perturbation approaches can be used for dissecting the necessity of regulatory elements.
source: Approaches that have shown the most success include the use of massively parallel reporter assays to examine allelic variation (Tewhey et al., 2016; Ulirsch et al., 2016; Vockley et al., 2015) and perturbation approaches for dissecting the necessity of regulatory elements (Canver et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2015; Fulco et al., 2016; Simeonov et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Genetic fine mapping approaches have improved the ability to identify putative causal variants among larger sets of variants in linkage disequilibrium.
source: In addition, genetic fine mapping approaches have improved our ability to identify putative causal variants among larger sets of variants in linkage disequilibrium (Guo et al., 2017; International Inflammatory Bowel Disease Genetics Consortium et al., 2017; Ulirsch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Putative causal variants most often localize to non-coding regions of the genome.
source: However, even when putative causal variants are identified at a disease or trait-associated locus, they most often localize to non-coding regions of the genome, making it difficult to connect variants to genes that mediate the observed effects in a scalable manner (Claussnitzer et al., 2015; Gupta et al., 2017; Smemo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies and represents established knowledge.

claim: GWAS studies have identified thousands of variants associated with various blood cell traits.
source: In the context of hematopoiesis, GWAS studies have identified thousands of variants associated with various blood cell traits, including hundreds associated with red blood cell traits alone (Astle et al., 2016; van der Harst et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published GWAS studies.

claim: BCL11A is a key regulator of fetal hemoglobin expression.
source: Thorough follow-up efforts at individual loci have identified important regulators of hematopoiesis, such as the key regulator of fetal hemoglobin expression, BCL11A (Basak et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2018; Sankaran et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The study focused on 75 loci associated with RBC traits identified by a GWAS performed in up to 135,000 individuals.
source: We focused on 75 loci associated with RBC traits that were identified by a GWAS performed in up to 135,000 individuals (van der Harst et al., 2012) spanning 6 RBC traits (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the source of the loci used in the study, supported by citation.

claim: The 75 loci have been robustly replicated in more recently reported association studies performed on larger cohorts.
source: Importantly, these 75 loci have been robustly replicated in more recently reported association studies performed on larger cohorts and thus represent important targets for perturbation studies (Astle et al., 2016; Ulirsch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to more recent GWAS studies.

claim: Each of the 75 sentinel SNPs was expanded to a linkage disequilibrium (LD) block including all SNPs in high LD (r2 >0.8).
source: To do this, each of the 75 sentinel SNPs was first expanded to a linkage disequilibrium (LD) block including all SNPs in high LD (r2 >0.8, Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), then further to the nearest genomic recombination hotspot.
evidence: This describes the computational method used to define genomic regions.

claim: Each gene was expanded to include a wingspan encompassing 110 kb upstream and 40 kb downstream of the transcriptional start and end sites.
source: Based upon insights from previous expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) studies (Montgomery and Dermitzakis, 2011; International Inflammatory Bowel Disease Genetics Constortium et al., 2011; Veyrieras et al., 2008), each gene annotated in the genome was expanded to include a wingspan encompassing 110 kb upstream and 40 kb downstream of the transcriptional start and end sites, respectively, to also capture potential functional regulatory elements.
evidence: This describes the method used to define gene regions, informed by cited eQTL studies.

claim: 389 genes overlapping or in the vicinity of the LD blocks were selected to be tested in the pooled loss-of-function screen.
source: This resulted in selection of 389 genes overlapping or in the vicinity of the LD blocks to be tested in the pooled loss-of-function screen.
evidence: This describes the outcome of the gene selection process.

claim: The genes were distributed at a median of 4 genes per loci.
source: These were distributed at a median of 4 genes per loci (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the gene selection process, shown in a figure.

claim: The approach may miss genes targeted by a trait-associated regulatory element in cases of long-range interactions.
source: This approach may on occasion miss genes targeted by a trait-associated regulatory element. For example, our approach would miss long-range interactions, as is observed at the FTO locus with IRX3/IRX5 (Claussnitzer et al., 2015; Smemo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an acknowledged limitation of the method, supported by citations to examples.

claim: LD and related metrics will only nominate a fraction of potential regulatory targets.
source: It is becoming increasingly clear that LD and related metrics will only nominate a fraction of potential regulatory targets (Whalen and Pollard, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: The majority of common genetic variation underlying RBC traits appears to act in a cell-intrinsic manner within the erythroid lineage.
source: Since the majority of common genetic variation underlying RBC traits appears to act in a cell-intrinsic manner within the erythroid lineage, we decided to perturb the candidate genes during the process of human erythropoiesis (Giani et al., 2016; Sankaran et al., 2012; Sankaran et al., 2008; Ulirsch et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: shRNA-based approaches in primary CD34+ HSPC-derived erythroid cells have been successful in validating individual genes underlying RBC traits.
source: First, we have had prior success validating individual genes underlying RBC traits using shRNA-based approaches in primary CD34+ HSPC-derived erythroid cells and our results have been consistent with orthogonal CRISPR based approaches (Giani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work from the authors.

claim: shRNA libraries can be much more efficiently packaged into lentiviruses and delivered to primary HSPCs compared to alternative CRISPR/Cas9-based guide RNA libraries.
source: Second, shRNA libraries can be much more efficiently packaged into lentiviruses and delivered to primary HSPCs compared to alternative CRISPR/Cas9-based guide RNA libraries (Ting et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents a technical consideration.

claim: All-in-one CRISPR or CRISPRi lentiviral constructs produce low titer viruses and require very high multiplicities of infection.
source: We observe that all in one CRISPR or CRISPRi lentiviral constructs that are ideal for primary HSPC screens produce low titer viruses and require very high multiplicities of infection that can be challenging to achieve for a pooled functional screen (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is an observation from the authors' experiments shown in a figure.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 based approaches can produce non-uniform loss-of-function or gain-of-function outcomes due to unpredictable DNA repair processes.
source: Third, the shRNA approach avoids potential complications like non-uniform loss-of-function or gain-of-function outcomes produced by CRISPR/Cas9 based approaches due to unpredictable DNA repair processes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) (Mandegar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation and data shown in a figure.

claim: shRNAs can act rapidly to achieve gene knockdown and thereby avoid compensatory effects that can occur when complete CRISPR knockout is achieved.
source: Furthermore, shRNAs can act rapidly to achieve gene knockdown and thereby avoid compensatory effects that can occur when complete CRISPR knockout is achieved (Rossi et al., 2015), better recapitulating the subtle changes in gene expression that are characteristic of common genetic variation.
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents a theoretical advantage.

claim: The pooled shRNA library consisted of 2803 hairpins targeting the 389 GWAS-nominated genes, along with 30 control genes.
source: Mobilized peripheral blood-derived primary human CD34+ HSPCs from three independent healthy donors were infected with a lentiviral-based pooled shRNA library consisting of 2803 hairpins targeting the 389 GWAS-nominated genes, along with 30 control genes (Moffat et al., 2006).
evidence: This describes the composition of the experimental library.

claim: Each GWAS-nominated gene was targeted with 5-7 distinct shRNAs.
source: Each GWAS-nominated gene was targeted with 5–7 distinct shRNAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design, shown in a figure.

claim: An infectivity of 35-50% was achieved.
source: Using lentiviral libraries with defined titers, we achieved an infectivity of 35–50%, which provides a good tradeoff between reasonably high infection while minimizing the possibility of multiple integrations per cell that can lead to combinatorial phenotypes.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: At least 1000 CD34+ HSPCs per hairpin were infected (7 ~ 11 * 10^6 cells per experiment).
source: To achieve sufficient library representation, we infected at least 1000 CD34+ HSPCs per hairpin (7 ~ 11 * 106 cells per experiment).
evidence: This describes the experimental scale.

claim: Hairpins targeting potential regulators of erythropoiesis would be depleted or enriched during the three-phase erythroid culture.
source: We hypothesized that hairpins targeting potential regulators of erythropoiesis would be depleted or enriched during the three-phase erythroid culture, similar to our prior experience in analyzing specific GWAS-nominated genes (Giani et al., 2016; Sankaran et al., 2012; Ulirsch et al., 2016).
evidence: This is the hypothesis of the study, informed by prior work cited.

claim: Genomic DNA was isolated and deep-sequenced from the pool of infected cells at six different culture time points.
source: To assay these hairpins, we isolated and deep-sequenced genomic DNA from the pool of infected cells at six different culture time points that represent distinct stages of erythropoiesis to most broadly assess putative causal genes that may act across the span of differentiation (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This describes the experimental method.

claim: Greater than 95% of hairpins were represented at levels of at least five log2 counts per million (CPM) at day 4.
source: Greater than 95% of hairpins were represented at levels of at least five log2 counts per million (CPM) at day 4, two days post-infection (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the sequencing data shown in a figure.

claim: A diversity of effects - in terms of both increased and decreased hairpin abundance - were observed across the two-week time course.
source: Across the two-week time course, a diversity of effects - in terms of both increased and decreased hairpin abundance - were observed.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Hairpins targeting genes with known biological roles in erythropoiesis, such as GATA1 and RPS19, showed markedly decreased abundance across the time course.
source: Hairpins targeting genes with known biological roles in erythropoiesis, such as GATA1 and RPS19 (Khajuria et al., 2018; Ludwig et al., 2014), showed markedly decreased abundance across the time course.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data, with citations supporting the known roles of these genes.

claim: Hairpins targeting a set of broadly essential genes were strongly depleted by day 16 when compared to negative control hairpins.
source: Likewise, hairpins targeting a set of broadly essential genes (Figure 1—source data 2) were strongly depleted by day 16 when compared to negative control hairpins targeting non-human genes, which showed little if any change (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The trends were recapitulated with strong correlation in each of the three donor CD34+ cell backgrounds.
source: These trends were recapitulated with strong correlation in each of the three donor CD34+ cell backgrounds (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation about reproducibility across replicates, shown in a figure.

claim: A linear mixed model was implemented to account for the longitudinal nature of the time course data.
source: A linear mixed model was implemented to account for the longitudinal nature of the time course data (Li et al., 2015) and to handle the confounding off-target and efficiency effects inherent to the shRNA modality (Riba et al., 2017; Tsherniak et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the statistical method used, supported by citations.

claim: Absolute hairpin abundances at each time point were converted to a log2 fold change relative to the initial hairpin abundances at the start of the differentiation.
source: Since we wanted our model to be able to detect significant changes in hairpin abundance at any time point throughout the differentiation process, we converted the absolute hairpin abundances at each of the six time points to a log2 fold change relative to the initial hairpin abundances at the start of the differentiation.
evidence: This describes the data transformation used in the analysis.

claim: Genes were called as hits if they had a fitted slope >0.1 log2 fold change per day within the interval while simultaneously possessing a Wald chi-square FDR-adjusted q value < 0.1.
source: Specifically, genes were called as hits if they had a fitted slope >0.1 log2 fold change per day within the interval while simultaneously possessing a Wald chi-square FDR-adjusted q value < 0.1.
evidence: This describes the statistical criteria for calling hits.

claim: This approach identified 77 genes at 38 of the 75 targeted loci which, when suppressed, had a significant effect on the slope of shRNA-encoding DNA abundance at any point during the time course.
source: In total, this approach identified 77 genes at 38 of the 75 targeted loci which, when suppressed, had a significant effect on the slope of shRNA-encoding DNA abundance at any point during the time course.
evidence: This is the primary result of the statistical analysis.

claim: A majority of the hit loci (27 loci) had 1-2 gene targets prioritized.
source: A majority of these hit loci (27 loci) had 1–2 gene targets prioritized (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the results, shown in figures.

claim: The candidate genes were found to be distributed across all 6 of the originally annotated RBC GWAS traits.
source: These candidate genes were found to be distributed across all 6 of the originally annotated RBC GWAS traits (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is an observation about the distribution of hits, shown in a figure.

claim: Hairpins targeting the hit genes showed strong internal consistency.
source: and hairpins targeting them showed strong internal consistency (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an observation about the quality of the hits, shown in a figure.

claim: The hit set was enriched for erythroid essentiality as quantified in the K562 erythroid cell line.
source: A permutation comparing the sum of K562 essentiality scores for the hit genes with those of randomly drawn, identically-sized gene sets from the library of targeted genes revealed that the hit set was indeed enriched with p=0.0269 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a validation finding using permutation analysis and external data.

claim: When compared to permuted sets of 77 genes randomly chosen from the genome, there was even stronger enrichment for erythroid essentiality with p=0.00021.
source: Likewise, when compared to permuted sets of 77 genes randomly chosen from the genome (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), there was even stronger enrichment for erythroid essentiality with p=0.00021
evidence: This is a validation finding using permutation analysis.

claim: The hit set was significantly enriched when compared to genes from libraries nominated by SNPs associated with lipid levels.
source: We further explored whether the enrichment could be due to an intrinsic bias inherent to GWAS screening itself by permuting sets of genes from libraries nominated by SNPs associated with low-density lipoprotein levels, high-density lipoprotein levels, and triglyceride levels, finding the hit set to be significantly enriched in all comparisons (Global Lipids Genetics Consortium et al., 2013) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: This is a validation finding using permutation analysis with external GWAS data.

claim: Five 'gold standard' genes in the library possess known genetic underpinnings via identified causal variants: CCND3, SH2B3, MYB, KIT, and RBM38.
source: We further validated the ability of this approach to discover genetically relevant hits by performing a permutation analysis based upon five 'gold standard' genes in the library, which possess known genetic underpinnings via identified causal variants: CCND3 (Sankaran et al., 2012; Ulirsch et al., 2019), SH2B3 (Giani et al., 2016), MYB (Galarneau et al., 2010; Sankaran et al., 2013; Sankaran et al., 2011), KIT (Jing et al., 2008; Ulirsch et al., 2019), and RBM38 (Ulirsch et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies for each gene.

claim: Enrichment for the five gold standards was seen with p=0.0249.
source: Calculating the rank sums of hairpins ordered by our model's computed FDR scores for 1,000,000 random combinations of five genes from the library yielded a distribution over which enrichment for the five gold standards was seen with p=0.0249 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a validation finding using permutation analysis.

claim: Among the 389 GWAS-nominated genes in the library, 20 (~5%) were found to contain at least one coding variant with a minimum posterior probability of association of 0.1.
source: Among the 389 GWAS-nominated genes in our library, 20 (~5%) were found to contain at least one coding variant from this list.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from analysis of fine-mapped variants.

claim: There was a significant enrichment of coding variants observed among the hits (~9%, p=0.03907).
source: Of these, there was a significant enrichment observed among the hits (~9%, p=0.03907 as determined by permutation analysis; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a validation finding using permutation analysis.

claim: Common myeloid progenitors (CMPs) and megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitors (MEPs) were significantly enriched for hit gene expression (p<0.01).
source: In the more holistic hematopoiesis dataset, common myeloid progenitors (CMPs) and megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitors (MEPs) were significantly enriched for hit gene expression (p<0.01).
evidence: This is a finding from expression analysis using external datasets.

claim: Proerythroblast, early basophilic, and late basophilic erythroblast stages were particularly enriched for hit gene expression (p<0.001).
source: Within a more detailed and separate analysis of human adult erythropoiesis, proerythroblast, early basophilic, and late basophilic erythroblast stages were particularly enriched (p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from expression analysis using external datasets.

claim: None of the 77 shRNA screen hits emerged using eQTLs located within the LD blocks of the original 75 sentinel SNPs from the GTEx whole blood dataset.
source: To examine how our results compare to target gene identification through eQTL-based approaches, we also examined the whole blood eQTL dataset form the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) Project, finding that none of the 77 shRNA screen hits emerged using eQTLs located within the LD blocks of the original 75 sentinel SNPs (GTEx Consortium, 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison with external eQTL data.

claim: The shRNA screen was performed on differentiating erythroid progenitors which are essentially not present in whole blood.
source: This is not entirely surprising given that the shRNA screen was performed on differentiating erythroid progenitors which are essentially not present in whole blood, so one would expect to miss cell type-specific effects or eQTLs that act in early progenitor populations.
evidence: This is an inference about why the eQTL comparison showed no overlap.

claim: STRING interaction network analyses identified underlying networks between hits in the screen.
source: Using STRING interaction network analyses (version 10.5) (Szklarczyk et al., 2017), we used empirical, database-curated, co-expression, genomic proximity, and text-mined evidence to identify underlying networks between hits in the screen.
evidence: This describes the network analysis method used, supported by citation.

claim: The networks highlighted interacting biological processes including cell signaling and transcription, cytoskeletal and membrane structure and function, and mRNA translation.
source: These networks highlighted a number of interacting biological processes of both known and previously unappreciated importance to erythropoiesis (Figure 4), including cell signaling and transcription, cytoskeletal and membrane structure and function, and mRNA translation.
evidence: This is a finding from network analysis shown in a figure.

claim: MYB is a master regulator transcription factor that has been implicated in playing a role in fetal hemoglobin regulation and in erythropoiesis more generally.
source: MYB is a master regulator transcription factor that has been implicated in playing a role in fetal hemoglobin regulation and in erythropoiesis more generally (Mucenski et al., 1991; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The MYB locus has been associated with numerous red blood cell traits.
source: The MYB locus has been associated with numerous red blood cell traits (including mean corpuscular volume, mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration, and RBC count) (Sankaran et al., 2013; van der Harst et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to GWAS studies.

claim: ETO2 (CBFA2T3) is a part of the erythroid transcription factor complex containing TAL1 and is required for expansion of erythroid progenitors.
source: ETO2 (CBFA2T3) is a part of the erythroid transcription factor complex containing TAL1 and is required for expansion of erythroid progenitors (Goardon et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Stem cell factor receptor KIT and erythropoietin receptor (EPOR) mediated signaling are essential for erythropoiesis.
source: Both stem cell factor receptor KIT and erythropoietin receptor (EPOR) mediated signaling are essential for erythropoiesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: CCND3 fills a critical role in regulating the number of cell divisions during terminal erythropoiesis.
source: CCND3 fills a critical role in regulating the number of cell divisions during terminal erythropoiesis and has been validated as a causal gene associated with variation in RBC counts and size (Sankaran et al., 2012; Ulirsch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: SLC4A1, also known as band 3, serves as a key component of the RBC membrane skeleton.
source: Our method recovered characteristic RBC genes like solute carrier family 4 member 1 (SLC4A1), also known as band 3, (Peters et al., 1996), which serves as a key component of the RBC membrane skeleton.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Ankyrin 1 (ANK1) is a direct interacting partner for SLC4A1 which anchors the cytoskeleton and cell membrane.
source: Likewise, it recovered a direct interacting partner for SLC4A1, ankyrin 1 (ANK1), which anchors the cytoskeleton and cell membrane (Bennett and Stenbuck, 1979)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: N-ethylmaleimide Sensitive Factor (NSF) facilitates membrane vesicle trafficking within the cell.
source: as well as N-ethylmaleimide Sensitive Factor, vesicle fusing ATPase (NSF), which facilitates membrane vesicle trafficking within the cell (Glick and Rothman, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: RPL7A and RPL19 have been implicated by mutations observed in studies of Diamond-Blackfan anemia.
source: Both RPL7A and RPL19, for instance, have been implicated by mutations observed in studies of Diamond-Blackfan anemia (Gazda et al., 2012; DBA Group of Société d'Hématologie et d'Immunologie Pédiatrique-SHIP et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Common genetic variation affecting ribosomal protein genes might contribute to the incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity of anemia seen in Diamond-Blackfan anemia patients.
source: The common genetic variation affecting these ribosomal protein genes might contribute to the incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity of anemia seen in Diamond-Blackfan anemia patients (Ulirsch et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: Common genetic variants may influence phenotypic outcomes in patients with neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: Similar effects have been reported in neurodevelopmental disorders, where common genetic variants may influence phenotypic outcomes in patients (Niemi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Exosome component 9 (EXOSC9) has been suggested to act as part of the exosome complex as a specific gatekeeper of terminal erythroid maturation.
source: Exosome component 9 (EXOSC9), for instance, has been suggested to act as part of the exosome complex as a specific gatekeeper of terminal erythroid maturation (McIver et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: TFR2 encodes a protein canonically involved in iron homeostasis that has recently been shown to also regulate EPO receptor signaling.
source: The first, transferrin receptor 2 (TFR2), encodes a protein canonically involved in iron homeostasis that has recently been shown to also regulate EPO receptor signaling (Forejtnikovà et al., 2010; Nai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: TFR2 has been studied in the context of murine erythropoiesis, but its role in human erythropoiesis has not been assessed.
source: Although TFR2 has been studied in the context of murine erythropoiesis, its role in human erythropoiesis has not been assessed.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature.

claim: Significant knockdown of TFR2 was observed at both the mRNA and protein levels using two independent shRNAs.
source: Significant knockdown of TFR2 was observed at both the mRNA (Figure 5A) and protein levels (Figure 5B) using two independent shRNAs from among the six targeting TFR2 in the screen.
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in figures.

claim: Downregulation of TFR2 increased erythroid differentiation as observed by increased expression of erythroid-specific cell surface markers CD235a and CD71 at day 9 and day 12 of culture.
source: Downregulation of TFR2 increased erythroid differentiation as observed by increased expression of erythroid-specific cell surface markers CD235a and CD71 at day 9 (shLUC ~22%; TFR2 sh1 ~42%; TFR2 sh2 ~40%) and day 12 of culture (shLUC ~60%; TF2 sh1 ~80%; TFR2 sh2 ~80%) (Figure 5C and E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in figures.

claim: Downregulation of TFR2 improved the later stages of erythroid differentiation/maturation, as observed by loss of cell surface marker CD49d at day 15 of culture, an increased rate of enucleation, and through assessment of cell morphology.
source: Downregulation of TFR2 also improved the later stages of erythroid differentiation/maturation, as observed by loss of cell surface marker CD49d at day 15 of culture, an increased rate of enucleation, and through assessment of cell morphology (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in figures.

claim: TFR2 has been isolated as a component of the erythropoietin (EPO) receptor complex.
source: Previous studies have reported the isolation of TFR2 as a component of the erythropoietin (EPO) receptor complex (Forejtnikovà et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: TFR2 downregulation resulted in significantly higher pSTAT5 phosphorylation in comparison to the control with EPO stimulation from 0.02 U/mL to 200 U/mL.
source: TFR2 downregulation resulted in significantly higher pSTAT5 phosphorylation in comparison to the control with EPO stimulation from 0.02 U/mL to 200 U/mL (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in a figure.

claim: The maximal pSTAT5 response could be achieved within a shorter period of EPO stimulation upon TFR2 downregulation.
source: In addition, the maximal pSTAT5 response could be achieved within a shorter period of EPO stimulation upon TFR2 downregulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in a figure.

claim: TFR2 is a negative regulator of EPO signaling.
source: Given our findings that TFR2 is a negative regulator of EPO signaling, it may be an ideal therapeutic target for conditions characterized by ineffective erythropoiesis like β-thalassemia (Rund and Rachmilewitz, 2005).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data, with citation to background on β-thalassemia.

claim: Tfr2 downregulation is beneficial in a mouse model of β-thalassemia.
source: A recent study has supported this hypothesis, showing that Tfr2 downregulation is beneficial in a mouse model of β-thalassemia (Artuso et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Extensive mRNA splicing occurs during the terminal stages of erythropoiesis.
source: Extensive mRNA splicing occurs during the terminal stages of erythropoiesis (Pimentel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: SF3A2 is a component of the U2SNRP complex whose binding to the branch point is critical for proper mRNA splicing.
source: SF3A2 is a component of the U2SNRP complex whose binding to the branch point is critical for proper mRNA splicing (Gozani et al., 1996; Gozani et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: SF3A2 was associated with maximal hairpin drop out at day 12 (FDR = 0.005).
source: SF3A2 specifically was associated with maximal hairpin drop out at day 12 (FDR = 0.005) – a later time point in erythropoiesis.
evidence: This is an observation from the screen results.

claim: Knockdown of SF3A2 in primary human CD34+ HSPCs results in decreased cell numbers during erythroid differentiation starting from day 7.
source: Knockdown of SF3A2 in primary human CD34+ HSPCs results in decreased cell numbers during erythroid differentiation starting from day 7 (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in figures.

claim: Decreased cell numbers were associated with decreased erythroid differentiation as measured by erythroid surface markers CD71 and CD235a.
source: Decreased cell numbers were associated with decreased erythroid differentiation as measured by erythroid surface markers CD71 and CD235a (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in a figure.

claim: An increase in non-erythroid lineages based on surface marker expression of CD11b (myeloid) and CD41a (megakaryocytic) was observed upon SF3A2 knockdown.
source: We also observed an increase in non-erythroid lineages based on surface marker expression of CD11b (myeloid) and CD41a (megakaryocytic) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in a figure.

claim: Cells treated with shRNA to suppress SF3A2 were found to differentially express 6061 genes with an adjusted p value < 0.05 as compared to the shLuc control.
source: Cells treated with shRNA to suppress SF3A2 were found to differentially express 6061 genes with an adjusted p value < 0.05 as compared to the shLuc control
evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Only 807 genes were differentially expressed in MDS patients with SF3B1 mutations compared to those without.
source: whereas only 807 genes were differentially expressed given the same threshold cutoff in the MDS patients with an SF3B1 mutations compared to those without (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq analysis of MDS patient data.

claim: Genes from both the SF3A2 differentially expressed set and the SF3B1 differentially expressed set were significantly enriched for structural constituents of the ribosome.
source: Genes from both the SF3A2 differentially expressed set and the SF3B1 differentially expressed set were significantly enriched for structural constituents of the ribosome (p<3.2×10−44 and p<7.5×10-24, respectively) among other cellular components and functions (Figure 6—source data 3 and 4).
evidence: This is a finding from pathway enrichment analysis.

claim: Both SF3A2 and SF3B1 knockdown were found to exhibit a similar proportion of altered splicing events.
source: Examining differential splicing in the set of genes not differentially expressed in either condition, both were found to exhibit a similar proportion of altered splicing events, including alternative 3' splice sites, alternative 5' splice sites, mutually exclusive exons, and skipped exons (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a finding from splicing analysis shown in a figure.

claim: Sf3b1K700E cells show reduced erythroid differentiation and cell growth compared to wild-type cells infected with control non-targeting shRNAs.
source: Consistent with previous reports, we observed that Sf3b1K700E cells show reduced erythroid differentiation and cell growth compared to wild-type cells infected with control non-targeting shRNAs (Figure 6F,G, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in figures.

claim: Downregulation of Sf3a2 using two independent shRNAs further worsens the defects in both erythroid differentiation and cell growth observed for Sf3b1K700E cells.
source: Downregulation of Sf3a2 using two independent shRNAs further worsens the defects in both erythroid differentiation and cell growth observed for Sf3b1K700E cells (Figure 6F,G, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in figures.

claim: Modulation of SF3A2 could modify the alterations of erythropoiesis observed in the setting of somatic SF3B1 MDS-causal mutations.
source: This data suggest that modulation of SF3A2 could modify the alterations of erythropoiesis observed in the setting of somatic SF3B1 MDS-causal mutations.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: MDS with SF3B1 mutations is characterized by significant variation in the degree of anemia found at the time of presentation.
source: This form of MDS is characterized by significant variation in the degree of anemia found at the time of presentation (Chronic Myeloid Disorders Working Group of the International Cancer Genome Consortium et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: A coding SNP, rs25672, was identified in LD with the sentinel SNP at the locus, rs2159213 (r2 = 0.737675 in CEU 1000 Genomes phase 3).
source: We identified a coding SNP, rs25672, in LD with the sentinel SNP at the locus, rs2159213 (r2 = 0.737675 in CEU 1000 Genomes phase 3), in which SF3A2 was the only gene identified by the linear mixed model as a hit.
evidence: This is a finding from genetic analysis.

claim: The screen identified 77 gene hits at 38 of the original 75 loci used to design the library.
source: The screen identified 77 gene hits at 38 of the original 75 loci used to design the library.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary results.

claim: The hits had strongly amplified essentiality in erythroid cell lines.
source: Collectively, these hits had strongly amplified essentiality in erythroid cell lines
evidence: This is a validation finding.

claim: The hits included a significant proportion of known, genetically-linked 'gold standard' erythroid genes.
source: included a significant proportion of known, genetically-linked 'gold standard' erythroid genes
evidence: This is a validation finding.

claim: The hits were enriched for red blood cell trait-associated coding variants orthogonally identified through genetic fine-mapping.
source: and were enriched for red blood cell trait-associated coding variants orthogonally identified through genetic fine-mapping.
evidence: This is a validation finding.

claim: The network of interacting gene hits highlighted biological components and pathways including specific signaling and transcription factors, membrane and structural components, and components involved in mRNA translation.
source: From a holistic perspective, the network of interacting gene hits highlighted a number of high-level biological components and pathways important for erythropoiesis, including specific signaling and transcription factors, membrane and structural components, and components involved in mRNA translation.
evidence: This is a finding from network analysis.

claim: The hits identified by the screen did not overlap those that would be identified with eQTLs from whole blood.
source: It is interesting to note that the hits identified by our screen did not overlap those that would be identified with eQTLs from whole blood
evidence: This is a comparison with eQTL data.

claim: Studies of variation in developing hematopoietic cells may not be accurately reflected by studies of circulating blood cells.
source: which emphasizes how studies of variation in developing hematopoietic cells may not be accurately reflected by studies of circulating blood cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the eQTL comparison.

claim: SF3A2 and potentially other regulators such as some implicated mRNA translation factors may be key disease modifiers that alter the impaired erythropoiesis seen in diseases like MDS or Diamond-Blackfan anemia.
source: In addition, our studies suggest that at least SF3A2, and potentially other regulators such as some implicated mRNA translation factors, may be key disease modifiers that alter the impaired erythropoiesis seen in diseases like MDS or Diamond-Blackfan anemia.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental findings.

claim: For the approach to be useful to a given research question, a suitable system capable of modeling the trait/disease of interest must first exist.
source: We acknowledge for it to be useful to a given research question, a suitable system capable of modeling the trait/disease of interest must first exist, and for many cellular systems this is often challenging.
evidence: This is a discussion of the limitations of the approach.

claim: The use of shRNAs as the vehicle for perturbation carries the proclivity of shRNA to exert confounding off-target effects when compared to CRISPR-based methods.
source: Likewise, the use of shRNAs as the vehicle for perturbation carries with it unique challenges, chief among them the proclivity of shRNA to exert confounding off-target effects when compared to CRISPR-based methods.
evidence: This is a discussion of the limitations of the approach.

claim: The inclusion of appropriate controls, both at the experimental level and in modeling off-target contributors to observed phenotypic effects, provide an effective means to address off-target effects.
source: While this is true and unavoidable, the inclusion of appropriate controls, both at the experimental level and in modeling off-target contributors to observed phenotypic effects, provide an effective means to address this issue (Tsherniak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents a methodological consideration.

claim: The targets of identified non-coding variants are occasionally not within linkage disequilibrium blocks in the genome.
source: Finally, evidence has recently been published that the targets of identified non-coding variants are occasionally not within linkage disequilibrium blocks in the genome (Whalen and Pollard, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Gene-centric screens are valuable for GWAS follow-up.
source: Our data show that gene-centric screens are valuable for GWAS follow-up.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study.

claim: Gene-centric screens are not limited to red cell traits and may be useful for other human traits/diseases.
source: They are not limited to red cell traits and may be useful for other human traits/diseases, as has begun to be shown in diseases like type 2 diabetes (Thomsen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to work in another disease area.

claim: Data from gene-centric screens can be integrated with complementary insights gleaned from variant centric screens.
source: Data from such screens can be integrated with complementary insights gleaned from variant centric screens.
